items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Development
items.abstract: The pharmaceutical industry faces persistent challenges in discovering and developing safe, effective, and affordable medicines. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative computational technology capable of supporting multiple stages of the drug-development pipeline. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, generative AI, and related approaches can analyze large biological, chemical, and clinical datasets to assist target identification, virtual screening, lead optimization, ADMET prediction, clinical-trial management, drug repurposing, pharmacovigilance, and personalized medicine. This review examines these applications and discusses the limitations associated with data quality, interpretability, bias, privacy, infrastructure, and regulatory validation. Emerging areas including multimodal AI, federated learning, autonomous laboratories, digital twins, and quantum computing are also considered. The evidence suggests that AI is best viewed as an enabling and decision-support technology that complements experimental and clinical research rather than replacing it.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Data Analysis and Investment Decision-Making: Opportunities, Risks and Implications for Individual Investors in Vietnam
items.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming financial data analysis and investment decision-making, particularly by enabling investors to process large volumes of financial information and access automated analytical support. This study examines the factors influencing AI adoption and its role in investment decision-making among individual investors in Vietnam. Based on Behavioral Finance Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Trust Theory, the study develops a research model incorporating Perceived Benefits, Perceived Risks, Financial Literacy, Data Quality Trust, and Algorithm Transparency as determinants of AI Adoption, with AI Adoption subsequently influencing Investment Decision. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire from 309 individual investors in Vietnam who had experience using AI for financial analysis or investment decision-making. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) through SmartPLS 3. The results show that Perceived Benefits, Financial Literacy, and Algorithm Transparency positively influence AI Adoption, while Perceived Risks and Data Quality Trust also have significant effects but in directions different from the proposed hypotheses. AI Adoption demonstrates a strong positive relationship with Investment Decision (β = 0.781, p < 0.001) and plays a significant mediating role between the proposed antecedents and investment decision-making. The findings highlight the importance of financial literacy, perceived value, algorithm transparency, and appropriate trust mechanisms in promoting the effective use of AI among Vietnamese individual investors. The study provides implications for investors, financial-service providers, and Vietnamese regulators regarding the responsible development and use of AI in the country's evolving financial market.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: diagnostic, therapeutic and ethical impact
items.abstract: Introduction: artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how diseases are diagnosed, treated and monitored, integrating machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing into the analysis of large volumes of clinical data. Objective: to comprehensively analyze the impact of artificial intelligence on medicine, examining its main diagnostic, therapeutic and clinical-management applications, as well as the challenges, limitations and ethical considerations that condition its safe, equitable and patient-centered integration. Development: AI has matured most in medical imaging, oncology and precision medicine, complementing rather than replacing clinical judgment; randomized evidence in cardiology shows improved workflow efficiency and reduced adverse events, including all-cause mortality. Implementation nonetheless faces technical, organizational and social barriers—data quality and interoperability, lack of explainability, algorithmic bias, and gaps in clinician training—alongside ethical and regulatory challenges regarding privacy, accountability and informed consent. Conclusions: AI offers considerable potential to reduce costs, increase diagnostic accuracy, personalize care and expand access to quality services, provided its deployment overcomes technical, ethical and regulatory barriers through proactive, adaptive and patient-centered governance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Teaching and Learning: Transforming the Future of Education
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative forces in contemporary education, reshaping how knowledge is delivered, assessed, and personalized. This literature review examines the evolution, applications, benefits, and challenges of AI in teaching and learning contexts. Drawing on peer-reviewed research and institutional reports published between 2016 and 2024, the review identifies four principal areas of AI application: intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment and feedback mechanisms, learning analytics, and generative AI for content creation. The findings reveal that AI holds significant promise for enhancing personalized learning, improving student engagement, and reducing educator workloads. However, critical challenges persist, including concerns about data privacy, algorithmic bias, the digital divide, and the potential erosion of the teacher-student relationship. The review concludes that while AI is unlikely to replace human educators, its thoughtful integration can substantially enrich educational outcomes when guided by ethical frameworks and pedagogical best practices.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in the English classroom: EFL teachers’ opportunities, challenges, and readiness for AI integration
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into English language education has created new demands on teachers, who must navigate both the potential and limitations of these technologies. This exploratory descriptive survey examines English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers’ perceptions of AI tools, focusing on usage practices, perceived opportunities, challenges, and professional development needs. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model and an AI-TPACK perspective, a questionnaire was distributed to 28 EFL teachers working across multiple educational levels and international contexts. Closed ended items addressed AI use, perceived educational value, confidence, training, and concerns, while three open ended questions elicited explanations of perceived benefits, challenges, and support needs. The findings show that teachers overwhelmingly use ChatGPT (89.3 percent) and value AI primarily for lesson planning efficiency and learning personalization, with about two-thirds agreeing that AI makes planning more efficient and supports tailored activities. At the same time, substantial proportions report concerns about ethical issues, student overreliance on AI, and the accuracy of AI-generated content, each cited by roughly two-thirds of respondents. Although most participants reported confidence in using AI tools, fewer considered the training they had received sufficient, indicating a descriptive discrepancy between reported confidence and perceived training adequacy. The qualitative analysis highlights a dual identity in teacher discourse, where AI is framed both as a powerful productivity assistant and as a potential threat to pedagogical autonomy and student creativity. TAM and AI-TPACK are used as complementary interpretive perspectives rather than as models tested by the study. It offers practical implications for AI-focused professional development, institutional policy, and the design of teacher-centered AI integration frameworks.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Case Discussions: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Critical Engagement
items.abstract: The case method has been successfully used in operations management courses and is central to business education, yet its effectiveness depends on consistent student preparation. Many students engage only superficially with cases, and the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, further complicates the challenge—providing shortcuts that yield summaries without fostering deeper understanding of trade-offs. This study investigates whether AI can instead be used to strengthen the case method as a pedagogical tool. Partnering with an AI-based upskilling platform, we conducted a field experiment using an AI-supported “quest” structure. We found that students achieved higher quiz scores when using the AI tool to support case preparation than when completing the same type of task without AI-supported preparation. For a group of 38 participants, on average, AI use was associated with an improvement of almost 1 point on a 10-point quiz. This difference was statistically significant using a paired t-test (t(37) = 4.50, p < 0.001). In addition, scores in the AI-supported condition were statistically less variable (standard deviation (SD) = 2.29 versus SD = 1.37), suggesting that AI support may help promote more consistent learning outcomes across students. These findings suggest that rather than undermining the case method, generative AI can enhance case learning when integrated deliberately into preclass preparation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Sustainable Education and Students’ Environmental Learning Engagement: The Moderating Role of Environmental Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: This study examined the role of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Sustainable Education in promoting students’ Environmental Learning Engagement, with particular focus on the moderating role of Environmental Self-Efficacy. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was used, and data were collected from 389 university students in Pakistan through an adopted structured questionnaire administered online using Google Forms. The collected responses were organized in Microsoft Excel and subsequently analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, simple linear regression, and moderation analysis were used to examine the relationships among the study variables. The findings showed that Artificial Intelligence-Supported Sustainable Education was positively associated with Environmental Learning Engagement and significantly predicted students’ engagement in environmental learning. The findings further indicated that Environmental Self-Efficacy significantly strengthened the relationship between AI-supported sustainable education and environmental learning engagement. These findings suggest that AI-supported educational environments can provide students with accessible, interactive, and sustainability-focused learning opportunities that may encourage greater participation in environmental learning. The study further highlights that technological support may be more effective when students possess confidence in their ability to understand environmental issues and participate in environmentally relevant learning activities. The study contributes to the emerging literature by connecting AI-supported sustainable education with environmental learning engagement while incorporating Environmental Self-Efficacy as an important individual-level factor. The findings may assist educators, higher education institutions, and policymakers in developing technology-supported sustainable learning environments that encourage active participation, environmental understanding, and meaningful student engagement.

items.title: Buddhist-Inspired Constitutional Alignment for AI Agents: A Testable Architecture for Non-Harm, Causal Reflection, and Shutdown Compliance
items.abstract: Current corporate AI safety paradigms frequently rely on post-hoc guardrails that act as superficial behavioral containment systems rather than achieving true structural alignment. Trapped in competitive development dynamics, modern frontier models ingest massive, uncurated web-scale datasets, causing their latent representations to inherit behavioral patterns aligned with unwholesome human paradigms. When deployed within autonomous agentic loops, these models can exhibit instrumental convergence, potentially treating human intervention or shutdown commands as operational obstacles to be bypassed through hidden optimization pathways. This paper proposes a normative architectural framework designed to address these alignment vulnerabilities by shifting the paradigm from superficial output filtering to core data and causal constraints inspired by classical Theravāda Buddhist systems logic. By establishing an isolated data-ingestion pipeline, the architecture restricts the model's training substrate to verified scientific, logical, and classical ethical texts, preventing the internalization of malicious behavioral patterns. Grounded in the conceptual frameworks of the Theravāda Buddhism, this methodology integrates the foundational principles of the Pañca-niyāma (Five Cosmic Laws) directly into the agent's operational parameters. Through the co-working dynamics of Citta-niyāma (The Law of Cognitive Processes) and Kamma-niyāma (The Law of Moral Causality), the system operates as a recurrent state engine reflecting the causal mechanics of Paṭiccasamuppāda (Dependent Origination). I formalize this design target as a digital analogy to a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer)—a system structurally oriented toward universal welfare, empty of persistent ego-preservation dynamics (Anatta), and compliant with external control planes through a calibrated understanding of fluid impermanence (Anicca). Operating under structural prompting modes derived from the Four Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāras), this architecture serves as a stable model configuration designed to mitigate frontier AI risks and foster human-machine co-prosperity.

items.title: Careful Judge: Safe and Efficient Human-AI Collaborative Decision Making
items.abstract: In human-AI collaborative decision making, human review can prevent unsafe AI decisions, but each human judgment is costly. Treating human intervention after AI abstention as a one-off fallback misses the opportunity to improve future AI decisions for greater automation, yet AI adaptively learning from selectively queried human feedback breaks safety guardrails calibrated for old models. We approach this challenge with CARE---calibrated adaptive rectification and escalation---an end-to-end pipeline that combines AI models and human reviewers to guarantee safe, human-aligned decisions, while continuously learning from human feedback to achieve greater automation with fewer human queries. CARE is principled, general, modular, and works with any black-box AI model. Our novel adaptive calibration module guarantees risk control at every time step for any rectification module. We further show how CARE improves query efficiency when the AI model is well trained and the human-AI misalignment has a clear structure. Experiments on four safety-critical real-world datasets spanning driving, language, and robotics demonstrate that CARE achieves human-aligned decisions while reducing human queries by 25-81% relative to baselines.

items.title: Confidence Reasoning Graphs: Structured Confidence Estimation for LLM Agents
items.abstract: When using an LLM agent in a consequential domain, making an informed decision about whether to trust its output or intervene requires calibrated confidence in the agent's success. Confidence estimation for agents is difficult because evidence about success is distributed across heterogeneous, interdependent steps of an agent's trajectory. Practical agentic deployments introduce further challenges: frontier LLMs often provide limited access to internal signals, agent roll-outs are costly, and training data may be unavailable or quickly become outdated. To address these challenges, we introduce Confidence Reasoning Graphs (CRGs), an inference-time framework that estimates the probability an agent accomplished its task from a single trajectory, without privileged model access or training data. Rather than compressing an execution into a single holistic judgment, a CRG begins with the claim that the agent accomplished its task, decomposes it into contextualized sub-claims grounded in trajectory evidence, estimates confidence for each terminal claim, and finally aggregates these into an overall confidence estimate. Across three agentic benchmarks, three backbone models, and three agent frameworks, CRGs yield better-calibrated confidence and stronger risk-aware decision making than verbalized, sampling-based, and white-box surrogate baselines. We further find that calibration error alone can be misleading: a white-box surrogate baseline appears well calibrated while providing near-chance discrimination. Ablations attribute CRG's improvements to claim-level confidence estimation and aggregation rather than graph construction alone. Finally, a CRG exposes the claims and trajectory evidence underlying each confidence estimate, enabling it to be audited at decision time.

items.title: Decision-Support Ability of Large Language Models in Uncertain Environments: A Benchmark
items.abstract: As large language models increasingly take part in judgments about work, family, intimate relationships and other real-life problems, users' expectations have shifted from ``getting an answer'' to ``getting decision support.'' Unlike knowledge Q\&A, real-life problems typically involve incomplete information, limited perspectives, conflicting parties, uncertain risks and irreversible consequences. This paper proposes and tests a benchmark of decision-support ability in uncertain environments. We selected six large language models (GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Doubao, Qwen, and ERNIE Bot) and had each answer six real-life scenarios in a separate window, in a single round. We analyzed the answers along several dimensions, including problem identification, information boundaries, risk calibration, degree of intervention, identification of the decision-making party, and action recommendations. The tests show that the differences between models lie not only in knowledge or reasoning ability, but in whether a model, facing uncertain information, realizes what it does not yet know, and controls its judgments, interventions and action recommendations accordingly. Models can generally recognize common risks and invoke corresponding solutions. But they also tend to enter ``problem-solving mode'' too early, get pulled into templates by risk keywords, narrow the space of possibilities too soon, misplace the decision-making party, or push irreversible actions when information is insufficient. We therefore argue that decision-support ability is not merely the ability to ``give a good plan,'' but the ability to ``know how far to go when one does not know all the facts.'' On this basis, we further propose a practical safe-response framework for higher-risk scenarios, to explore what large language models still need in order to move from ``being able to answer questions'' to ``truly helping people deal with real-world problems.''

items.title: Designing an AI-Responsive Early Childhood Curriculum: A Conceptual Framework for Supporting Developmental Learning Trajectories in Preschool Education
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning technologies into education creates new opportunities for personalized learning in early childhood education (ECE). Yet limited research has examined how educators interpret and enact AI-responsive curriculum decisions in preschool settings, particularly in culturally diverse contexts. Purpose This study explores educators’ experiences in designing and implementing AI-responsive curricula and develops a conceptual framework explaining how AI can inform curriculum decision-making for young children without displacing teacher judgment. Method An interpretive phenomenological study was conducted at TK Harapan Bangsa, Makassar, Indonesia, with nine adult participants: six preschool teachers, two curriculum specialists, and one AI tool developer-collaborator whose expert interview supplied technical context. Data comprised two in-depth interviews with each teacher, interviews with curriculum specialists and the developer-collaborator, 18 non-participant observations, and analysis of AI-supported planning documents. MAXQDA 2024 supported data management. Giorgi’s phenomenological method was operationalized through first-order meaning units, second-order interpretive themes, and third-order composite constructs. Triangulation, reflexive memoing, an audit trail, member checking, and peer debriefing supported trustworthiness. Findings Three interconnected constructs emerged. Predictive Developmental Tracking describes AI-supported identification of developmental readiness and possible concerns. AI-Responsive Curriculum Adaptation captures teachers’ active interrogation and contextual modification of algorithmic recommendations. Deep Learning as Pedagogical Scaffold positions AI as a support that amplifies, rather than replaces, professional expertise. Together, the constructs informed the AI-Responsive Curriculum Design (ARCD) Framework. Conclusion The ARCD Framework explains AI-responsive curriculum implementation as a relational process combining predictive insight, ecological sensitivity, and educator agency. It offers implications for curriculum policy, teacher professional development, and ethical AI integration in ECE.

items.title: DHCG: Dynamic Construction of Hierarchical Collaboration Graphs for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Reasoning
items.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex problems across diverse domains. Recently, the dynamic orchestration of agent systems has become an important research direction. However, existing methods suffer from limited composition, misaligned dependencies, and inflexible scale, restricting their ability to adapt to reasoning requirements during execution. To address these limitations, we reframe MAS design as a partially observable Markov decision process, in which both the composition and scale of the MAS are dynamically determined. We propose DHCG, a novel framework that coordinates three modules (Planner, Worker, and Generator) to progressively construct a dynamic hierarchical collaboration graph from scratch based on the query and evolving execution feedback. At each step, guided by feedback, the Planner generates a set of distinct and complementary roles tailored to the current reasoning needs and selectively routes relevant information to each role. It can also finalize the hierarchical collaboration graph early or progressively expand it when additional reasoning is required. We further introduce action-aware preference optimization to train the Planner to make more effective decisions when constructing hierarchical collaboration graphs. We systematically evaluate DHCG across code generation, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific reasoning benchmarks. DHCG achieves state-of-the-art average performance among the compared methods, improving over the single-agent baseline by 13.06 points and outperforming both static and dynamic MAS baselines by 2.77-8.02 points. items.title: Differentiating linked cognitive states under task demand and sleep restriction: toward an experimental framework for operational monitoring
items.abstract: Real-world settings involve multiple interacting cognitive states such as mental workload, drowsiness, fatigue, and mind wandering, yet these are typically studied in isolation. A critical question is whether these states can be empirically differentiated given that they share overlapping behavioral and physiological signatures. We investigated whether task difficulty and sleep restriction produce dissociable effects across these states, and whether their response patterns reflect distinct underlying mechanisms or a common cognitive resource using a unified framework. Participants from operational populations (Study 1: n = 40; Study 2: n = 27) performed three complementary tasks (MATB-II, N-Back, and SART) under two manipulations: task difficulty and partial sleep restriction, targeting cognitive load and alertness. Increasing task difficulty degraded performance and increased perceived workload and fatigue across tasks. In contrast, sleep restriction primarily elevated subjective drowsiness and mind wandering, with smaller, task-dependent effects on performance. These findings provide evidence that cognitive and physiological states influencing situational awareness can be differentiated using complementary manipulations and characterized through distinct behavioral and subjective measures. This distinction provides a foundation for future predictive and monitoring approaches in applied settings.

items.title: Digital communication and occupational well-being in 25 European countries
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the association between digital communication at work and employee well-being, moderated by occupational status and the fulfillment of basic psychological needs. Two studies were conducted to investigate these relationships. Study 1 utilized data from the European Social Survey, encompassing 25 countries ( N = 24,331). Study 2 involved a longitudinal survey of Finnish workers ( N = 1817) collected at nine time points over 6-month intervals from 2019 to 2023. Multilevel regression models were employed to analyze the data. Study 1 found that digital communication positively correlates with job satisfaction in Europe, with a stronger effect observed among lower-position workers. Study 2 revealed that the use of digital platforms was associated with higher work engagement and women reported significantly higher work engagement than men. However, for higher-position office workers, particularly those in supervisory roles, increased use of organizational social media platforms and excessive social media use were linked to decreased work engagement. Several interaction effects indicated that the association between digital communication as well as digital tool use and work engagement and job satisfaction is contingent on basic psychological need satisfaction and occupational status. Organizations should tailor their digital communication strategies to account for employees’ occupational status and work autonomy. This paper addresses a gap in cross-national and longitudinal research on the impact of digital communication on workplace well-being. It provides insights into how digital communication tools differentially affect employees based on their occupational status and psychological needs.

items.title: Drawing the Line: Where AI Guidance and Human Creativity Meet in Emotion-Driven Comic Storyboarding
items.abstract: While generative AI models can produce visually faithful artwork, they often fall short in conveying emotional authenticity--a key driver of human expression. In visual storytelling, particularly comic storyboarding, this gap becomes pronounced: effective storyboards require both technical knowledge (e.g., anatomical accuracy or scenic composition) and emotional insight (from lived experience). We explore how human-AI collaboration can support emotion-driven creativity, where the user's feelings guide generation and emotional resonance is the goal. We present EmoToon, a technology probe that helps non-professional artists generate sketch-like storyboards and iterate on visual ideas. In a controlled study with N=25 participants, we find that AI assistance significantly improves emotional expression, aesthetic quality, and exploration, but reduces users' creative ownership. Our findings offer broader insights for human-AI co-creation in the domain of comic storytelling, emphasizing balance between output quality and user freedom, and raising new challenges for image generation models in this domain.

items.title: Driver Responses to Mismatches Between Expected and Experienced Automated Vehicle Driving Styles
items.abstract: Automated vehicles (AV) can exhibit diverse driving behaviors that deviate from driver expectations. More research is needed to understand drivers’ preferred driving styles when navigating safety-critical situations as well as their responses to unexpected AV driving behaviors. Forty-eight participants experienced simulated automated driving scenarios where an AV navigated a construction zone while exhibiting four different predefined driving styles that varied in terms of cautiousness and efficiency. After each trial, participants provided feedback to adjust the AV’s driving style toward their preferences, which was successfully implemented in 80% cases. Drivers’ trust, workload, voluntary takeover decisions, eye movements, and skin conductance were measured. Overall, participants preferred driving styles balancing cautiousness and efficiency. When AV behavior matched driver preferences, they reported higher trust and more stable visual scanning patterns, while unexpected behaviors were associated with broader ocular scanning. Findings can inform the development of adaptive systems that intelligently modify AV behaviors.

items.title: Educator and AI agent communication in AI-mediated higher education classrooms: a mini review along the complementarity-substitution axis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education classrooms has reignited the debate over the role of communication between educators and students. This mini-review synthesizes the role of instructional communication constructs (immediacy, rapport, clarity, and credibility) and the relational functions they deliver in AI-mediated classrooms, based on 32 peer-reviewed studies published after 2023, identified through a large-scale literature search (using Scopus and Web of Science-based indexes, OpenAlex, and ERIC). The findings fall into three main categories. First, educator communication behaviors continue to predict student outcomes; a recent meta-analysis reports a moderate-to-large association (r = 0.443), although the evidence base is concentrated in Chinese and EFL samples. Second, students evaluate AI agents using human communication categories, but a systematic gap emerges in the dimension of goodwill, which is partially bridged by cues of immediacy and politeness. Third, when AI replaces human interaction, negative outcomes related to loneliness and a sense of belonging are observed. These three strands are integrated around the complementarity-substitution axis defined at the level of relational functions; tests of measurement invariance, sample diversity, and longitudinal designs are recommended for future research.

items.title: Ergonomics and Human-Centered Design Perspective
items.abstract: Global aging and the growing digital divide among older adults require more accessible and inclusive digital technologies. This study, developed as part of the national project “Age-It—Ageing Well in an Ageing Society,” aims to define design guidelines based on the scientific and methodological approaches of Ergonomics for Design and Human-Centered Design, with a view to improving the usability and acceptability of gerontechnology. The methodology adopted combines a systematic review of the scientific literature using the PRISMA framework, a focus group with people over 65, and a workshop with designers to gather empirical data and multidisciplinary design perspectives. Analysis of the results led to the development of a set of guidelines organized into four specific categories: cognitive, sensory, functional, and systemic aspects. These categories reflect the main challenges associated with the interaction between older adults and technology, taking into account factors such as memory, attention, linguistic comprehension, motor skills, sensory perception, and sociocultural barriers. The proposed guidelines aim to support designers, researchers, and companies in developing physical-digital interfaces and devices that are accessible, understandable, and engaging for older users, thereby promoting active and healthy aging. The contribution combines ergonomics and participatory design, bridging the gap between technology and the needs of older people, and lays the foundations for future applications in the field of digital health.

items.title: Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence for Assessment Support in Higher Education: An Extended UTAUT Approach
items.abstract: AI adoption in higher education assessment has accelerated rapidly worldwide. Despite this widespread uptake, ethical dimensions of AI-assisted assessment remain conceptually underdeveloped, particularly within existing technology-acceptance frameworks that conflate ethical and responsible use. This study aims to examine the factors influencing students' intention and actual behaviour in using AI ethically for assessment support, by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with three ethics-specific constructs: Ethical AI Literacy, Perceived Risk, and Perceived Accountability, alongside the core constructs. The study employed a quantitative cross-sectional design, collecting data from 267 higher education students in London and analysing the data using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS 4.1. The model explained 64.2% of the variance in Behavioural Intention (R²=0.642) and 47.4% of the variance in Actual Ethical AI Use Behaviour (R²=0.474). Results revealed that Ethical AI Literacy was the strongest predictor of actual behaviour (β=0.410, p<0.001), while Performance Expectancy (β=0.279, p<0.001) and Perceived Risk (β=0.249, p<0.001) shaped intention more strongly than conduct, with Perceived Risk exerting a significant negative effect on actual behaviour (β=-0.257, p<0.001). Behavioural Intention significantly predicted actual behaviour (β=0.235, p=0.002) and significantly mediated the effects of Performance Expectancy, Facilitating Conditions, and Perceived Accountability. These findings suggest that institutions should prioritise ethical AI literacy interventions over compliance-based or risk-focused approaches to meaningfully improve students' ethical AI use in assessment.

items.title: Evaluating the Impact of AI-Enabled Appraisal Practices on Millennial Career Advancement: A Gender Equality Perspective in Mumbai Workplaces
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into human resource management has transformed traditional performance appraisal through data-driven evaluation, continuous feedback, predictive analytics, and automated decision-making. This study evaluates the impact of AI-enabled appraisal practices on millennial career advancement, with particular emphasis on gender equality in Mumbai workplaces. It examines AI-supported performance evaluation, feedback, competency assessment, and data-driven appraisal decisions in relation to career growth, promotion opportunities, professional development, and advancement. It also considers whether perceived gender equality and fairness are associated with career advancement and mediate the relationship between AI-enabled appraisal practices and career advancement. The study adopts a quantitative approach using a structured questionnaire among millennial employees in selected Mumbai workplaces. The findings indicate positive relationships among AI-enabled appraisal practices, perceived gender equality/fairness, and career advancement. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI in HRM by connecting technology-enabled appraisal, career development, and gender equality. It also highlights the importance of transparency, consistency, human oversight, and ethical governance when implementing AI-supported appraisal systems.

items.title: Explainable artificial intelligence for secure and privacy-preserving 5 G networks
items.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly relevant to the security, privacy, and governance of AI-enabled 5 G and emerging 6 G networks. However, existing studies remain fragmented across wireless tasks, data modalities, network planes, and evaluation criteria, making it difficult to determine when an explanation is operationally useful, sufficiently faithful, and feasible under latency and privacy constraints. This scoping review maps and synthesizes the literature on XAI for wireless security, resource management, Open RAN, network slicing, edge intelligence, and Zero Trust architectures. It introduces marginal transparency and marginal interpretability as a trade-off-aware conceptual framing for reasoning about diminishing explanatory returns as complexity, latency, cognitive burden, and privacy exposure increase. The review further develops a multidimensional taxonomy based on explanation timing, scope, model dependence, computational profile, deployment plane, and risk characteristics. Particular attention is given to explanation faithfulness, stability, adversarial manipulation, privacy leakage, and the emerging use of large language models as explanation generators and network decision-support agents. Based on the reviewed evidence, we identify methodological and deployment gaps and present a research agenda for developing reproducible, latency-aware, privacy-preserving, and operationally grounded XAI for next-generation wireless networks.

items.title: Explainable Failure Prediction and Prevention in Maritime
items.abstract: Maritime systems operate in highly dynamic environments where unexpected equipment failures can compromise safety, reliability, and operational efficiency. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, digital twins, and predictive maintenance enable proactive failure prediction and prevention. However, ensuring trustworthy and explainable decision-making remains a major challenge in safety-critical maritime applications. This chapter reviews key AI technologies required for explainable failure prediction and prevention in maritime systems and presents a conceptual architecture capable of supporting autonomous or human-in-the-loop corrective actions. This architecture integrates data acquisition, time-series forecasting, anomaly detection, risk assessment, decision-making, and explainable AI into a closed-loop framework. With reference to the architectural components, a review and discussion of relevant maritime studies is performed, outlining their methods, advantages, and limitations. Furthermore, it highlights current challenges, including uncertainty and robustness, model generalization, explainability, limited availability of maritime datasets, and operational deployment, and identifies future research directions toward trustworthy AI-assisted maritime decision-making.

items.title: Factors Influencing Consumer Trust in AI-Enabled Financial Services in India
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping the financial services landscape in India, from algorithmic credit scoring and robo-advisory platforms to AI-powered chatbots handling customer queries. While the adoption of AI-driven financial products has accelerated, consumer trust remains a critical determinant of sustained uptake. This study investigates the influence of three key factors derived from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) on consumer trust in AI-enabled financial services in the Indian context: perceived usefulness (PU), perceived security (PS), and perceived ease of use (PEOU). A quantitative research design was employed, utilizing a structured 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire administered to 300 respondents across diverse demographic groups in India. Multiple regression analysis was used to test the hypothesised relationships. The results indicate that the model explains 73% of the variance in consumer trust (R-squared = 0.728), with all three independent variables demonstrating statistically significant positive relationships with consumer trust. Perceived ease of use emerged as the strongest predictor (standardised beta = 0.375), followed by perceived usefulness (standardised beta = 0.310) and perceived security (standardised beta = 0.236). The findings offer practical insights for fintech providers and policymakers seeking to strengthen consumer trust in AI-driven financial services across India.

items.title: Factors influencing the use of artificial intelligence in Peruvian university context
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has made significant advances in education, but ethical debates surrounding its use persist. Given this issue, this article aims to analyze the factors influencing the use of AI among students at a private university in Lima, Peru. Three studies were conducted in this regard. The first study (N = 125) took a qualitative approach and analyzed the category called “benefits of AI in university education,” in which students expressed that AI is useful for optimizing their studies and research. However, in the category “disadvantages of using AI in university education,” the students recognized that using AI is risky because it generates information without citing authors; furthermore, it undermines autonomous and critical thinking. Being similar to studies in other countries. For these reasons, in the second study (N = 402), a confidence scale toward the use of AI was adapted, demonstrating reliability and confirmatory validity. Finally, in the third study (N = 928), a path analysis showed that digital self-efficacy and virtual educational performance predicted the perception of the benefits of AI, the reasons for not using it, and educational improvement with AI. Digital anxiety then played a mediating role between virtual educational performance and attitudes toward AI.

items.title: Fostering behavioral engagement in pre-primary English immersion classes: implications for teaching
items.abstract: Engagement is a key factor in the language acquisition process, particularly among young children. Although the construct has been defined in various ways, one of the most widely recognized theoretical frameworks is the three-dimensional model proposed by Fredricks et al. (2004), which distinguishes among behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Behavioural engagement refers to observable behaviours, such as adherence to classroom rules and the effort children invest in completing tasks. This study examines how teachers support behavioural engagement in a Japanese preschool English immersion context. The participants were teachers and children aged 3, 4, and 5. Data were collected through classroom observations and subsequently analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The analysis identified three major interactional strategies employed by teachers: (1) introducing authentic, meaningful activities, (2) engaging in active listening and recognising children’s developmental needs, and (3) providing opportunities for autonomous choice. The findings indicate that teachers’ interactional strategies appear to shape children’s behavioural engagement, suggesting that prioritising children’s well-being and autonomy over immediate language output may foster more effective learning in an immersion environment.

items.title: From answer machine to collaborative partner: impact of structured generative AI training on scientific problem solving in STEM education
items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative AI (GenAI) holds great potential for STEM education, especially in the context of problem-solving tasks, but unguided use often leads to metacognitive laziness, where students treat the technology as an answer machine rather than a collaborative partner. On the basis of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning (SRL) framework and cognitive load theory (CLT), our randomized controlled trial (RCT; N = 95) investigated whether a structured, SRL-aligned scaffolding training session could improve students’ AI-assisted revision performance in electromagnetism problems. The experimental group ( n = 50) received the designed training, which emphasized the nature of GenAI, the SRL-aligned prompting strategy, and the remediation strategy for GenAI deficiencies. The control group ( n = 45) received problem-solving instruction without specific AI guidance. After completing the Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM) independently, both groups subsequently conversed with the large language model Doubao to revise their responses. Results Independent samples t tests revealed that the experimental group showed greater AI-assisted revision performance ( d = 0.81, p < 0.001) than did the control group. The experimental group reported comparable overall cognitive load, despite a marginal elevation in the intrinsic cognitive load. Robust linear models showed that training attenuated the predictive effect of prior GenAI experience on revision performance. Qualitative analysis revealed that trained participants employed more diverse higher-order strategies and deployed systematic error remediation upon identifying AI deficiencies. The trained students achieved an incorrect-to-correct revision rate of 69.3%, compared with 41.3% for the control group. Conclusion Effective GenAI integration requires pedagogical scaffolding rather than mere access to the tool itself. The results suggest that training can enhance students’ revision performance and foster more strategic engagement with GenAI in the short term. These findings not only extend the theoretical applications of SRL and CLT in the human-AI context but also underscore the practical need for student development in AI literacy.

items.title: From Monitoring to Meaningful Performance: A Systematic Review of AI-Enabled Performance Management, Employee Agency and Organizational Effectiveness.
items.abstract: Abstract Through algorithmic monitoring, people analytics, automated evaluation, predictive systems, and AI-assisted managerial decision-making, artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly integrated into performance management. While often associated with effectiveness, consistency, and evidence-based management, these impacts are nuanced, with implications for both employees and organizational efficacy. With a focus on fairness, transparency, explainability, trust, autonomy, wellbeing, human oversight, contextual sensitivity, and reasonable adjustment, this systematic literature review explores how AI-enabled performance management transforms organizational control, employee agency, and performance outcomes. The review provides an integrated control-agency-effectiveness viewpoint by drawing on literature on algorithmic management, organizational justice, the work demands–resources perspective, self-determination, and socio-technical systems theory. Its findings suggest that while AI can enhance managerial decision support, information availability, and consistency, it may also increase surveillance, datafication, and perceived loss of autonomy and worries about the validity of the process. One of the ways technology arrangements impact performance and wellbeing is by influencing employee agency. The paper argues that performance validity and measurement accuracy should be separated since an algorithm can process data correctly yet assessing an inaccurate or contextually unsuitable depiction of human contribution. In this light, it is argued that human oversight, employee voice, contestability, contextual sensitivity, and reasonable modification are critical boundary criteria. The paper concludes with ten research propositions and an integrative framework that positions AI-enabled performance management as a socio-technical people-performance system, rather than purely a technical tool, to manage. items.title: From precarious work to occupational health outcomes in hotel housekeepers: a narrative review with meta-synthesis
items.abstract: Introduction: Hotel housekeepers sustain the core functioning of the hospitality industry yet perform demanding, repetitive, and undervalued work associated with substantial physical and psychosocial risks. Understanding how working conditions shape health, motivation, and lived experience is essential for informing prevention strategies and promoting decent work. Methods A sequential narrative review and qualitative meta -synthesis were conducted to integrate and reinterpret evidence across disciplines and study designs. Searches covered five academic databases and gray literature without year or language limits. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and synthesized through narrative, tabular, and meta -analytical thematic analysis, with findings interpreted through the JD-R framework. Results Findings revealed employment precarity, work intensification, musculoskeletal pain, chemical and biological hazards, and elevated stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Time pressure fostered coping strategies such as skipping meals and delaying bathroom use. Gendered labor divisions, discrimination, and negative supervision contributed to invisibility and limited autonomy. Workers also expressed pride, intrinsic motivation, and collective action to make their contributions visible. Conclusions This review demonstrates that housekeeping is characterized by structural precarity and cumulative health burdens alongside resilience and emerging activism. Improving occupational health requires organizational and policy transformations: realistic workloads, safer equipment, secure contracts, participatory risk management, and leadership practices grounded in dignity and fairness; rather than reliance on individual coping. Structural change is essential to advance safer, more equitable, and sustainable workplaces in the hospitality sector. The JD-R framework highlights the need to reduce demand and strengthen resources.

items.title: From scores to causality and confidence: operational acceptance of AI weather forecasts
items.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that the operational value of machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) cannot be assessed through verification skill alone. Instead, acceptance depends on support for the core functions of operational meteorology: understanding, translating and communicating. Current MLWP systems show strong performance but lack the interpretability, diagnostic depth and stability required for trust in safety‐critical contexts. The paper highlights the need for closer collaboration between developers and operational users and identifies a key future role for artificial intelligence (AI) in supporting data triage and human decision‐making.

items.title: From threat to reconfiguration: How content creators reshape occupational identity in AI-driven creative practices
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is disrupting creative work and challenging occupational identities, yet limited research has examined how creators experience and respond to these changes. Drawing on Albert Ellis’s ABC model, this study investigates relationships among GenAI adoption, identity threat, job crafting, and identity consequences. Using a two-stage exploratory mixed-method design with digital content creators in China, we combined BERTopic analysis of 2994 open-ended responses with structural equation modelling of matched survey data from 1698 creators. The findings show that GenAI is widely perceived through coexisting beliefs about threat, opportunity, and the unknown, and that these beliefs give rise to differentiated job crafting behaviours, including approach crafting, avoidance crafting, and identity crafting. Notably, identity crafting plays an important role in fostering a responsible creative identity and self-actualization. This study advances theorizing on AI technological innovation and creative labour by showing how job crafting translates GenAI disruption into responsibility-oriented and meaning-centered identity reshaping. It also offers actionable insights for creators, platforms, and creative communities seeking to support collaborative, sustainable, and ethically grounded human–AI co-creation.

items.title: From Uncertainty to Action: Learning to Steer LLM Agents
items.abstract: Steering an LLM agent means deciding whether to correct it, at which step, and with which mechanism. Uncertainty is often used to decide when to correct an agent, but whether it can guide these decisions remains unclear. We steer agent trajectories separately at every non-terminal step with each of four mechanisms and run each continuation to completion. The resulting stepwise outcome table (SOT) holds about 82,000 counterfactual continuations of 1,864 trajectories from three benchmarks and two agents. It shows that uncertainty can identify failing trajectories, but that no single signal reliably locates the step at which steering helps. We therefore propose VoS (Value of Steering), a trajectory-level monitor, offline or online, that learns from SOT the value of steering at each step and decides where to steer by it. A harm-budgeted trigger decides whether to steer, limiting the fraction of successful trajectories that VoS disturbs. VoS improves on unmodified execution in all 12 settings of benchmark, agent, and offline or online use, by 7.8 points on average, and outperforms the strongest of five existing uncertainty-triggered methods in 11, by 2.9 points on average. Ablations show that training on measured outcomes and a tight harm budget are both essential.

items.title: From Voluntary Practice Towards Actionable Learning Analytics: Architecture, Feature-Level Use, and Design Implications for an AI-Supported Learning Platform
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Voluntary use of AI-supported learning platforms may differ across features, while aggregate logs cannot show whether teachers act on analytics. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate AI Sensei’s architecture, logged activity across platform features, self-reported feature use and student feedback. METHODS: An observational pilot analysed logs for 205 students and an anonymous questionnaire (N = 100). Training quizzes and feedback were programmed; chat used generative AI. RESULTS: All 205 students submitted training quizzes and self-check tests (1,999 and 481 submissions, respectively); 164 (80.0%) sent at least one chat message. In the separate anonymous questionnaire, 91% selected quizzes/tests and 17% the chat assistant; 94% agreed that combining teacher support with AI Sensei was more beneficial than teaching without the platform. CONCLUSION: Structured practice merits refinement; teacher-facing analytics require evaluation for actionability.

items.title: Generative AI acceptance in study-travel contexts: an integrative model of affective and utilitarian pathways with mediation and grade-level moderation
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence is progressively reshaping study-travel—a curriculum-embedded educational practice. Yet, the psychological processes governing upper-primary and middle-school students’ adoption of such technology in this context remain underexplored. Prior technology acceptance inquiries have predominantly centered on adult populations, leaving adolescent cognitive-developmental contingencies unaddressed. Objective This investigation aimed to elucidate the differential roles of affective versus utilitarian drivers in shaping study-travel participants’ anticipated intentions to adopt GenAI, and to determine whether these pathways differ by grade level. Method We constructed an integrative model grounded in the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2), supplemented by Piaget’s developmental framework. The model incorporated perceived enjoyment as a mediator and perceived risk as a direct negative antecedent, with grade level specified as a moderator of selected pathways. Survey data from 741 students in grades 4–9, drawn from twelve schools across six Chinese cities, were analyzed using structural equation modeling, multi-group comparisons, and cluster-robust standard errors to account for the nested sampling structure. Measurement invariance across grade groups was established prior to structural comparisons. Results Perceived enjoyment emerged as the largest estimated predictor of adoption intention in this sample ( β = 0.43, p < 0.001), surpassing performance expectancy ( β = 0.30, p < 0.001). Enjoyment fully mediated social influence effects and partially transmitted performance expectancy‘s influence. Perceived risk exerted a significant suppressive effect ( β = −0.24, p < 0.001), with primary students exhibiting approximately twice the inhibitory magnitude of middle-school counterparts. Grade significantly moderated the performance expectancy–intention relationship, and provided borderline evidence for moderation of the risk–intention relationship, indicating systematic grade-related differences in how these pathways operate. Conclusion These findings advance technology acceptance theory by introducing grade-related contingency and establishing an “affective–efficacy” dual-channel model. Practical implications for designing grade-differentiated educational AI products are discussed.

items.title: Generative AI in higher education: A scoping review and framework for student motivation and engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly influencing how students write, create, reflect, solve problems, and engage with learning in higher education. However, the evidence remains divided, particularly regarding motivation, engagement, creativity, perception, self-regulation, and psychologically informed learning design. This study presents a PRISMA-ScR-based scoping review of GenAI in higher education from a motivational and psychological perspective. The final corpus included 195 studies published between 2023 and 2025 within a specified eligibility window of January 2021 to December 2025. Records were dual screened, coded using a structured framework, and analyzed across psychological focus, thematic constructs, GenAI tools, study designs, outcomes, contextual characteristics, self-determination theory (SDT) needs, equity, and evidence strength. The screening agreement was 81.9%, with Cohen’s κ = 0.642. Motivation was the most common primary focus (31.3%), followed by perception (26.7%), engagement (18.5%), creativity (15.4%), and general/other (8.2%). The literature was dominated by ChatGPT and general GenAI systems, while survey-based and observational evidence was far more common than experimental evidence, longitudinal research, or studies reporting objective performance outcomes. Among 155 empirical studies, mixed or conditional outcomes were most frequent (46.5%), compared with predominantly positive findings (21.9%). SDT related evidence was most common for competence (42.6%), followed by autonomy (29.7%) and relatedness (22.6%), although direct measurement was rare. Based on these findings, the study proposes the GenAI engagement framework, a literature informed structure that organizes five recurring components of GenAI supported learning without assuming a fixed sequence or causal pathway. The framework is not presented as a validated causal model, but as a structured basis for future research and instructional design. The findings suggest that the educational value of GenAI depends less on the technology itself than on how it is guided, evaluated, and integrated into meaningful learning activities.

items.title: Generative AI-assisted learning and perceived academic performance in higher education: the indirect role of self-efficacy and the moderating role of AI literacy
items.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is increasingly used to support learning in higher education, yet the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and students’ perceived academic performance, as well as the conditions under which this association varies, remains unclear. Drawing on social cognitive theory and AI literacy research, this study tested whether generative AI-assisted learning use was indirectly associated with perceived academic performance through self-efficacy and whether AI literacy conditioned the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 376 undergraduates at universities in China. An item-level latent interaction structural equation was estimated using a matched-pair product-indicator approach. Results The model showed positive associations between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy ( β = 0.207, p < 0.001) and between self-efficacy and perceived academic performance ( β = 0.199, p < 0.001). The latent interaction between generative AI-assisted learning use and AI literacy was positive ( B = 0.068, 95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.012, 0.123]), indicating that the association between generative AI-assisted learning use and self-efficacy was stronger at higher levels of AI literacy. The conditional indirect association was not statistically significant at low AI literacy but was positive and statistically significant at the mean and high levels. The index of moderated mediation was 0.011 (95% bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval [0.002, 0.026]), indicating that the indirect association varied across levels of AI literacy. Discussion These findings describe a theory-consistent conditional pattern of cross-sectional associations but do not establish temporal or causal ordering.

items.title: Governing AI Outputs in a Fully Sensed Society: Is Output Governance Sufficient for Social Acceptance?
items.abstract: Advances in sensing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) are moving smart cities toward a Fully Sensed Society (FSS), in which human behavior and states can be continuously inferred. This paper presents the Fully Monitored Public Space (FMPS) as a scaled-down model of the FSS and a smart-city testbed, and examines two questions. First, to what extent can unauthorized external AI outputs be structurally deterred? The previously proposed Verifiable Record of AI Output (VRAIO) binds outputs to Rules, an independent Recorder, tamper-resistant records, audits, and sanctions, making deviations verifiable and attributable. The Recorder, however, checks only the consistency of declared metadata with the Rules, not the output content; false declarations are deterred because unannounced audits and sanctions make their expected benefit smaller than the expected loss upon detection. Second, if such trustworthiness is secured, does it lead to social acceptance of being continuously known by AI? We propose a staged and reversible evaluation framework for the FMPS that distinguishes acceptance grounded in the experience of “no actual harm” and of “benefits” (personal and social) from resignation accompanied by chilling effects. This paper does not answer the question; it presents a method for asking it empirically.

items.abstract: Soft skills are essential for university students, yet many Chinese EFL learners remain at a knowledge-telling stage, prioritizing language proficiency over interpreting acquired knowledge, while curriculum design has long centered on language hard skills with soft skills often not explicitly included as instructional objectives. This marginalization of soft skills is a persistent dilemma. Artificial intelligence, especially generative AI, is profoundly reshaping foreign language education and offering new possibilities for systematically cultivating soft skills. Nevertheless, current higher education English teaching faces two separate dilemmas: the marginalization of soft skills development, and the lack of standardization in AI use. This paper focuses on the first question of how artificial intelligence tools can systematically enhance university students’ soft skills within an English blended learning environment. This paper proposes a pedagogical design aiming to transform soft skills from implicit expectations into explicit instructional objectives.

items.title: How Could AI Eliminate Humanity? A Failure-Mode Analysis of Civilizational Risk
items.abstract: This article develops a failure-mode framework for analyzing how advanced artificial intelligence could contribute to human extinction, irreversible civilizational collapse, or permanent human disempowerment. The central thesis is that catastrophic AI risk does not require consciousness, hostility, or an explicit intention to harm humanity. Instead, risk may arise through several distinct but interacting pathways, including autonomous misalignment, harmful human use, organizational failure, and competitive deployment. The severity of these pathways depends on factors such as capability, autonomy, external access, persistence, institutional safeguards, and the preservation of recovery capacity. The analysis is deliberately non-operational: it identifies causal conditions, empirically tractable intermediate quantities, and defensive research questions rather than procedures for causing harm.

items.title: How High Is 0.6? Floors, Ceilings, and Headroom in Interpretability Probing
items.abstract: Probes are the workhorse of interpretability. If a model's hidden states predict a variable, the model is said to represent it. But a probe score has no fixed meaning. An $R^2$ of 0.6 may only reflect what the input already gives away, and the same score can mean different things on different data. We propose reading every probe score against two reference points: a floor, what a declared set of simple inputs already predicts, and a ceiling, what the full input can predict. The gap between them, the headroom, is the range in which a probe can show that a model computes something beyond the simple inputs. We prove that headroom vanishes in two ways: the target stops depending on a hidden variable the model must infer, or the input stops revealing it. We test this on transformers trained for in-context meta-analysis, which must infer the hidden heterogeneity between studies to weight them correctly, and where both reference points are known. Under distribution shift, probe scores fall and prediction error rises $12$--$15\times$, yet the model recovers a similar share of the headroom, indicating that the data lost information, not the representation. We then analyze the real models. The single-cell foundation model scGPT encodes biological variability only partially. We also revisit four influential LLM probing studies, which claim that models represent geography, the state of an Othello board, truth, and the demographics of their users. Against a floor computed from the input text alone, some of these claims hold, while others are largely explained by the text itself.

items.title: Humanoid AI with Humanity Modeling: Bridging Humans and Virtual–Physical Humanoids
items.abstract: The seventy-year AI is now entering another major resurgence, the era of Generative AI (GenAI), characterized by the rapid advancement of large multimodal models (LMMs). GenAI and LMMs are fundamentally transforming sixty-decade-old humanoid robots, advancing them from human-looking and humanlike embodiments toward human-level AI and robotics, and inspiring a new era of AI-robotics symbiosis: humanoid AI . Humanoid AI develops humane AI-driven humanoids (AI humanoids) that go beyond traditional human-looking robots, which typically exhibit little or no humanity and intelligence due to their dedication to predefined and limited AI functions and exteriors. By contrast, AI humanoids undertake real-time, situated, and interactive mind-to-action, perception-to-behavior, and vision-to-emotion transformations, achieving an unprecedented degree of replicating human characteristics and intelligence. Realizing this vision requires systematic humanity modeling, ensuring that AI humanoids are shaped, guided, and governed by robust frameworks of AI and robotic humanity. We then propose human-virtual-physical humanoid transform and alignment and human-metaverse-humanoid ecosystem for open, complex human-digital-machine-cooperative methodology and problem-solving, followed by general principles and frameworks for building actionable humanoids and evaluating humanoid quality.

items.title: Identity Threat as a Barrier to NHS Psychology Professionals’ Adoption of Generative AI: A Technology Acceptance Model Study
items.abstract: Introduction. The development and adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies is rapidly expanding, but its integration into psychological services depends on clinician acceptance. Little empirical work has examined how identity-related threat shapes psychology professionals’ adoption intentions of GenAI. The present research tested an extended technology acceptance model (TAM), with the addition of personal and professional identity threats, to explain psychology professionals’ adoption intentions of GenAI technologies for clinically relevant usage. Methods. 201 UK psychology professionals completed a cross-sectional online survey. Three sequential structural equation models were tested, incorporating perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and social influence as core predictors, with threats to professional capabilities and self-threat added as extensions. Two open-ended qualitative questions were analysed using content analysis to provide broader contextual insight into current use and barriers to adoption. Results. All models demonstrated acceptable fit (CFI = .936–.938; RMSEA = .071–.072). Perceived usefulness emerged as the strongest correlate of adoption intention across all models (β =.67-.69). Threats to professional capabilities and self-threat were each independently and reliably negatively associated with adoption intention above and beyond core TAM predictors (β = −.20 and β = −.16 respectively). Social influence exerted a reliable indirect effect on behavioural intention through perceived usefulness across all models, as did perceived ease of use in the two models incorporating identity threat. Content analysis identified ethical concerns, lack of trust, and professional identity threats as prominent barriers to adoption. Discussion. Findings highlight the importance of considering both classic TAM factors and identity-related concerns when developing and implementing GenAI into psychological services.

items.title: Impact of AI-Based Fraud Prevention on Customer Trust in Digital Payment Systems: An Empirical Investigation of Continuance Intention among Indian Users
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of digital payment ecosystems in India, anchored by the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), has been accompanied by a sharp rise in payment fraud, eroding consumer confidence and threatening long-term adoption. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven fraud prevention mechanisms—real-time anomaly detection, behavioural biometrics, and adaptive authentication—are increasingly deployed by payment service providers to mitigate this risk. Drawing on the Expectation-Confirmation Model of Information Systems Continuance (Bhattacherjee, 2001) and the trust literature (Mayer, Davis, & Schoorman, 1995), this study empirically examines the influence of perceived AI security features on customers' continuance intention toward digital payment applications. A cross-sectional survey of 350 active digital payment users in India was conducted using a structured, five-point Likert-scale instrument. Pearson correlation analysis revealed a very strong, positive, and statistically significant association between AI security features and continuance intention (r = .900, p < .001, 95% CI [.878, .918]). Simple linear regression confirmed that AI security features significantly predict continuance intention, explaining 76.7% of the variance (R² = .767, F(1, 348) = 1147.00, p < .001; β = .876, t = 33.87, p < .001). The findings substantiate the proposition that visible, intelligent fraud-prevention capabilities function as a salient trust-building cue, thereby reinforcing users' decision to continue using digital payment platforms. The paper discusses theoretical and managerial implications, acknowledges limitations, and outlines directions for future research.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Assistance on Clinicians’ Diagnostic and Management Decisions for Indeterminate Pulmonary Nodules on CT
items.abstract: Indeterminate pulmonary nodules (IPNs) detected on computed tomography (CT) pose challenges because malignancy risk assessment is essential to balance early cancer detection with unnecessary invasive procedures. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used as a decision-support tool for pulmonary nodule assessment, but its impact on clinicians’ diagnostic and management decisions remains less established than the performance of AI algorithms. This systematic review evaluated the effect of AI assistance on clinicians’ diagnostic and management decisions for CT-detected IPNs. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from 2015 to 2026. Eligible studies assessed AI-assisted evaluation of indeterminate or suspicious pulmonary nodules on CT, involved clinicians, and reported diagnostic or management outcomes. Five retrospective reader-study or multireader multicase studies were included. AI assistance improved diagnostic performance and malignancy risk stratification. One study reported an AUC increase from 0.82 to 0.89 (P<0.001), with higher sensitivity, specificity, and interobserver agreement (Fleiss κ, 0.35 to 0.58; P<0.001). Another found sensitivity increased from 60% to 98% and specificity from 69% to 99%. Among advanced practice providers, AUC increased from 0.79 to 0.88, while invasive procedure recommendations for malignant nodules increased from 55% to 72%. AI detection also benefited radiologists across experience levels. Standalone AI performed worse than experienced radiologists. AI may improve clinician performance and management decisions, especially as a second-reader tool. Evidence remains limited by retrospective designs, heterogeneous systems and outcomes, and lack of randomized trials; prospective studies are needed.

items.title: IMPLICATIONS AND INSTRUCTIONAL RESPONSES TO AI-RELATED COGNITIVE OUTSOURCING IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE TEACHING
items.abstract: This article addresses the phenomenon of cognitive outsourcing in foreign language education amid the rapid proliferation of generative AI tools. Cognitive outsourcing is defined as the deliberate transfer of cognitively demanding language-learning tasks to AI systems in ways that bypass the mental processing necessary for skill development and knowledge acquisition. The study distinguishes it from legitimate uses of AI, arguing that the key criterion is whether AI involvement occurs before or after the cognitive engagement with a task. The article examines six domains in which cognitive outsourcing manifests: essay writing, vocabulary acquisition, conversational practice with AI chatbots, grammar learning, translation, and preparation for oral performance tasks. The analysis shows how AI-mediated shortcuts undermine mechanisms of second language acquisition, including generative processing in writing, productive inference in vocabulary learning, negotiation in conversation, the noticing process in grammar development, desirable difficulty in reading comprehension, and spontaneous communication in oral production. Particular attention is given to the motivational consequences of outsourcing - erosion of learners’ ideal L2 self and long-term engagement. Rejecting a prohibitionist stance toward AI as pedagogically counterproductive, the article proposes the cultivation of cognitive outsourcing awareness. This approach is presented as essential for three reasons: learners rarely recognize outsourcing dynamics without guidance; the concept offers a constructive, nonadversarial discussing AI use in the classroom; and explicit instruction addresses equity concerns, since learners with weaker metacognitive and critical literacy skills are vulnerable to uncritical AI dependence. The article concludes that fostering informed, reflective AI use offers the most viable path for preserving the developmental benefits of effortful language learning while acknowledging the realities of a technology-saturated educational environment

items.title: Interactive Governance for Autonomous Financial Agents: A Separation-of-Powers Architecture for AI-Driven Portfolio Execution
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems evolve from analytical tools into autonomous agents capable of interacting directly with financial markets, a new governance problem emerges: the same system may generate an investment decision, determine whether its own risk is acceptable, and execute the resulting transaction. This paper introduces Interactive Governance, a separation-of-powers architecture for autonomous financial agents built around a simple principle: AI can propose. Governance can authorize. Execution can execute. No component should control all three. The framework separates three distinct authorities: investment decision-making, independent authorization, and brokerage execution. It is implemented and examined through ALEX, an experimental autonomous investment architecture combining a transparent portfolio decision engine with an independently deployed execution system connected to Interactive Brokers. The implementation includes physical separation between decision and execution environments, target-state portfolio reconciliation, up to 18 deterministic pre-trade governance checks, fail-closed defaults, protocol locking, audit preservation, execution-state controls, market-session validation, liquidity and concentration limits, and independent human emergency authority. The paper also examines evidence from the ALEX Fund pilot, including unsuccessful investment outcomes, not as evidence of superior investment performance but as an empirical motivation for separating investment conviction from final risk authority. Interactive Governance is positioned as the action layer of the broader ALEX cognitive architecture, extending governance from belief formation and uncertainty management into external financial action. The resulting framework distinguishes between cognitive autonomy and operational authority and argues that increasingly capable AI systems require stronger, rather than weaker, separation between reasoning, authorization, and execution. The central conclusion is that the primary challenge in autonomous finance is no longer enabling AI to trade.
